rows.evidence: Q1: section 'Farmers' rationale for using drip irrigation' - in-depth repeated interviews with 12 drip-adopting farmers in Bassi Tehsil, Jaipur District, in 2015 and 2016. Q2: same section - all 12 farmers reported no reduction in groundwater pumping time or schedules, and farmers said they use about the same amount of water or maybe more after drip; Conclusions state the case demonstrates intensification exacerbating groundwater over-extraction. Q4: same section - intermediate variables reported from interviews: share of cultivable area irrigated rose from about 40% before drip to 67% after; shift to water-intensive chilies and greenhouse off-season crops; 4 of 12 farmers added solar tube-wells to pump in addition to electric bore-wells. Q7: Abstract, Introduction and Conclusions - the authors state from their findings that in the absence of regulations over groundwater abstraction (regulatory institutional vacuum) farmers adopt drip to intensify rather than conserve, and that drip will not lead to water savings without new institutional arrangements (groundwater usage rules and laws).
rows.notes: Evidence on water use is farmer self-report from qualitative interviews, not measured pumping or groundwater levels; the paper cites GRACE and other groundwater data from other work for context, which does not count. Q4 marked yes because intermediate variables (irrigated area share, pumping schedules, crop choice) are reported from the study's own interviews, though not instrumentally measured. Q6 marked no: results are from 12 farms in one tehsil; statements about Rajasthan-wide over-extraction are extrapolation. Q8: only a generic call for more research on Jevons paradox drivers; no explicit statement of limitations of the small purposive sample or interview method. Q9: no dispersion for the result (only landholding range).

rows.evidence: Q1: section 'Farmers' rationale for using drip irrigation' - own interviews with 12 drip-adopting farmers, 2015 and 2016, Bassi Tehsil. Q2: same section and Discussion - farmers adopted drip to intensify and expand production, reported no reductions in pumping, were aware water demand was growing with negative impacts on groundwater recharge; authors conclude drip adoption in a regulatory vacuum is leading to continued or expanded groundwater extraction rather than savings. Q4: same section - irrigated share rose from about 40% to 67% of cultivable area; new water-intensive chili and greenhouse crops; additional solar tube-wells run alongside electric bore-wells. Q7: Abstract and Conclusions - authors state the outcome occurs in the absence of rules over groundwater abstraction and that water savings will not occur without new institutional arrangements.
rows.notes: Function is labelled groundwater_recharge but the passage's effect is excessive groundwater extraction, which the study addresses via farmer self-reports; recharge itself is not measured (only mentioned as farmers' awareness). Policy-document review (NMMI, Rajasthan State Water Policy) describes context, not a second method establishing the effect, so Q3 no. Groundwater over-extraction is not measured by the study; evidence is qualitative interviews in one administrative block.

rows.evidence: Q1: section 'Farmers' rationale for using drip irrigation' - interviews with 12 drip farmers in Bassi Tehsil, Rajasthan, 2015 and 2016. Q2: Discussion - authors state their findings demonstrate the Jevons paradox/rebound effect, where adoption of drip led to increased rather than decreased groundwater use; farmers reported no reduction in pumping and the same or more water used. Q4: 'Farmers' rationale' section - mechanism variables reported: irrigated area share rose from about 40% to 67%, reduced fallow via greenhouses, shift to water-intensive crops, extra solar pumping. Q7: Abstract and Conclusions - the rebound is stated to occur under absence of groundwater regulation and a political economy incentivizing intensification; savings require new rules.
rows.notes: The passage says the paradox has been observed in various contexts; this study provides one context (one tehsil, 12 farmers) and cites other contexts (Ward and Pulido-Velazquez 2008, Dumont et al. 2013) from other work, which does not count. Evidence is qualitative self-report, no measured water use; no triangulation, no dispersion, no explicit limitation statement beyond a call for further research.

notes: Full text appears complete. Qualitative political-ecology case study based on repeated interviews with 12 drip-adopting commercial farmers (purposive snowball sample, nearly the whole adopter population in Bassi Tehsil) plus review of Indian and Rajasthan policy documents. No instrumental measurement of water use or groundwater levels; results on increased water use rest on farmer statements and reported changes in irrigated area and cropping.
